title: Torit Mutiny Launches First Sudanese Civil War
description: Southern Sudanese soldiers of the Equatoria Corps mutinied at Torit on August 18, 1955, killing northern officers and sparking the First Sudanese Civil War months before Sudan's formal independence. The mutiny, rooted in southerners' fear of Arab-Muslim domination and broken promises of federation, marked the opening of a 17-year insurgency that would shape South Sudan's political identity for generations.

title: Sudan Independence — South Excluded from Power-Sharing
description: Sudan gained independence from Britain and Egypt on January 1, 1956, but southern leaders felt immediately marginalized as Khartoum reneged on pre-independence promises of a federal arrangement. The new Arab-dominated government in Khartoum offered no southern representation in the transitional cabinet, fueling the ongoing Anyanya insurgency in the South.

title: Military Coup in Khartoum Hardens Southern Marginalization
description: General Ibrahim Abboud seized power in Sudan in November 1958, suspending parliament and installing a military government that pursued aggressive Arabization and Islamization policies in the South. The imposition of Arabic as the official language of education in southern schools and the expulsion of Christian missionaries intensified southern resistance and recruitment into the Anyanya movement.

title: Anyanya Insurgency Escalates into Sustained Guerrilla War
description: The Anyanya ('snake venom') insurgent movement consolidated under various southern commanders and escalated its guerrilla campaign against the Sudanese army across the three southern provinces. Anyanya drew recruits from mutineers, displaced civilians, and Nile Anya tribesmen, and began receiving limited covert support from neighboring Uganda, Ethiopia, and Israel.

title: Juba and Wau Massacres of Southern Civilians
description: Sudanese army forces killed hundreds of southern civilians in Juba and Wau in response to Anyanya attacks, in one of the most documented atrocities of the First Civil War. The massacres galvanized southern opinion and increased refugee flows into Uganda, the Central African Republic, and Ethiopia, drawing international attention to the conflict.

title: Nimeiri's Coup and Initial Southern Overtures
description: Colonel Jaafar Nimeiri seized power in Khartoum in May 1969, initially adopting a more conciliatory stance toward the South than his predecessors by acknowledging southern regional distinctiveness. His government opened secret back-channel talks with southern leaders in exile, laying groundwork for eventual negotiations, although fighting continued.

title: Joseph Lagu Unifies Anyanya into SSLM
description: General Joseph Lagu brought the fragmented Anyanya factions under a single command structure as the South Sudan Liberation Movement (SSLM), creating a credible military and political interlocutor for peace negotiations with Khartoum. Israeli weapons and logistical support channeled through Uganda's Idi Amin strengthened the SSLM at a critical moment before peace talks.

title: Addis Ababa Agreement Ends First Civil War
description: The Addis Ababa Agreement, signed on March 27, 1972, ended the First Sudanese Civil War by granting the southern three provinces a single autonomous Southern Sudan Regional Government with its own legislature and executive. The agreement integrated Anyanya fighters into the Sudanese Armed Forces and ended 17 years of conflict, producing a decade of relative peace that became the benchmark for later negotiations.

title: Southern Sudan Regional Government Established in Juba
description: Abel Alier was elected President of the new High Executive Council governing autonomous Southern Sudan from Juba, with a regional assembly and a degree of self-rule unprecedented in Sudan's history. The post-Addis Ababa decade saw investment in Juba, integration of Anyanya into the military, and the return of hundreds of thousands of refugees.

title: Chevron Discovers Major Oil Fields in South Sudan
description: Chevron announced major oil discoveries in Bentiu (Unity State) in 1978, with subsequent finds extending through Upper Nile — placing the bulk of Sudan's oil wealth inside the South's territory. The discovery transformed the political economy of the North-South relationship, as Khartoum sought to redraw regional boundaries to bring oil fields under northern jurisdiction.

title: Nimeiri Abrogates Addis Ababa Agreement and Redivides South
description: President Nimeiri unilaterally abrogated the 1972 Addis Ababa Agreement in June 1983, dissolved the Southern Regional Government, and redivided the South into three smaller regions to weaken southern political cohesion and facilitate northern control of oil fields. The decision was the proximate trigger for the Second Sudanese Civil War.

title: September Laws: Nimeiri Imposes Sharia Nationwide
description: In September 1983, Nimeiri declared Sudan an Islamic state and imposed Sharia law nationwide — including in the predominantly Christian and animist South — ordering amputations, floggings, and alcohol bans. The September Laws were received as a profound assault on southern identity and drove mass recruitment to the new SPLA insurgency.

title: SPLA Founded by John Garang Following Bor Mutiny
description: Colonel John Garang led the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) and its political wing, the SPLM, following the mutiny of Battalion 105 at Bor in May 1983, transforming a local military uprising into a national insurgency. Garang framed the SPLA's goal as a 'New Sudan' of equal citizenship rather than outright secession, giving the movement broad ideological appeal while receiving critical support from Ethiopia's Mengistu government.

title: Nimeiri Overthrown; Transitional Government in Khartoum
description: General Abd al-Rahman Siwar al-Dhahab overthrew Nimeiri in a bloodless coup in April 1985 while Nimeiri was abroad, forming a Transitional Military Council that promised elections and peace talks with the SPLA. The SPLA refused a ceasefire and continued operations, skeptical of Khartoum's sincerity on the Addis Ababa Agreement's restoration.

title: Koka Dam Declaration — Peace Talks Stall
description: The SPLM/A and several northern opposition parties signed the Koka Dam Declaration in Ethiopia in March 1986, agreeing to repeal the September Laws and convene a national constitutional conference. Prime Minister Sadiq al-Mahdi's civilian government refused to endorse the declaration, and negotiations collapsed, allowing the civil war to intensify.

title: Al-Bashir's Islamist Coup Radicalizes Sudan
description: General Omar al-Bashir seized power on June 30, 1989, in a coup orchestrated with Hassan al-Turabi's National Islamic Front, ending civilian rule and installing an Islamist military government that pursued the war in the South with renewed ideological ferocity. Al-Bashir declared jihad against the southern insurgency, and the National Islamic Front militias (Popular Defense Forces) were deployed alongside the army.

title: SPLA Split: Nasir Declaration and Bor Massacre
description: Riek Machar, Lam Akol, and Gordon Kong issued the Nasir Declaration in August 1991, accusing Garang of autocracy and calling for southern independence rather than a 'New Sudan,' fracturing the SPLA into Garang's predominantly Dinka faction and Machar's predominantly Nuer SPLA-Nasir. Machar's forces subsequently massacred thousands of Dinka civilians in the Bor region in November 1991, embedding Dinka-Nuer ethnic enmity that would resurface fatally in 2013.

title: IGAD Peace Process Begins
description: The Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) launched a formal mediation process between Khartoum and the SPLM/A in 1993, establishing what became the main diplomatic framework for resolving the Second Civil War. Despite years of failed talks and periodic ceasefires, the IGAD process eventually produced the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, making it the most consequential diplomatic framework in South Sudan's path to independence.

title: Khartoum Peace Agreement with SPLA Factions
description: Khartoum signed peace agreements in 1997 with several breakaway SPLA factions including Riek Machar's South Sudan Independence Movement, creating the South Sudan Defence Forces allied with Khartoum. The agreements temporarily divided the southern resistance but failed to end the broader conflict, and Machar eventually rejoined Garang's SPLA in 2002.

title: Greater Nile Oil Pipeline Opens — War Financed by Oil
description: The 1,600 km Greater Nile Petroleum Operating Company pipeline, linking the Muglad Basin oilfields in the south to Port Sudan on the Red Sea, began operating in 1999 after construction through the late 1990s. Oil revenues — reaching over $1 billion annually by 2000 — allowed Khartoum to dramatically increase military spending, fund helicopter gunships, and intensify scorched-earth campaigns to depopulate oil-producing areas in the South.

title: US Envoy Danforth Appointed — Diplomatic Momentum Builds
description: President George W. Bush appointed former Senator John Danforth as Special Envoy for Sudan in 2001, injecting US pressure into the stalled IGAD peace process and conditioning normalization with Khartoum on progress toward a comprehensive settlement. Post-9/11 intelligence cooperation between Khartoum and Washington paradoxically accelerated peace diplomacy as al-Bashir sought to improve his international standing.

title: Machakos Protocol — Self-Determination Agreed in Principle
description: The government of Sudan and SPLM/A signed the Machakos Protocol in Kenya in July 2002, the first breakthrough agreement in IGAD negotiations, which recognized the right of southern Sudan to hold a self-determination referendum after a six-year interim period. The protocol established the framework for all subsequent negotiations leading to the CPA, and Machar's rejoining of the SPLA around this time reunified the main southern factions.

title: Darfur Conflict Erupts — Complicates CPA Talks
description: Non-Arab rebel movements in Darfur launched an armed uprising against Khartoum in 2003, and the government's brutal counter-insurgency using Arab Janjaweed militias drew international outrage and complicated the Sudan-SPLM peace negotiations. The parallel Darfur crisis absorbed diplomatic attention but also increased international pressure on Khartoum to conclude a deal with the South.

title: Comprehensive Peace Agreement Signed — Path to Independence
description: The Government of Sudan and the SPLM/A signed the Comprehensive Peace Agreement (CPA) in Nairobi on January 9, 2005, ending 22 years of civil war, establishing a six-year interim period, promising a southern self-determination referendum in 2011, and providing for revenue-sharing of oil receipts. The CPA created a Government of National Unity in Khartoum with SPLM participation and a semi-autonomous Government of Southern Sudan in Juba, and is considered the founding document of South Sudan's statehood.

title: John Garang Dies in Helicopter Crash — Salva Kiir Takes Over
description: SPLM/A leader John Garang died on July 30, 2005, just 21 days after being sworn in as Sudan's First Vice President, when his Ugandan presidential helicopter crashed in bad weather in the Imatong Mountains. His death triggered riots in Khartoum and Juba and removed the SPLM's most visionary leader; his deputy Salva Kiir Mayardit assumed the SPLA/M chairmanship and southern presidency, shifting movement politics toward Dinka ethnic consolidation and eventual separatism.

title: Government of Southern Sudan Established in Juba
description: The Government of Southern Sudan (GoSS) was formally established under the CPA with Salva Kiir as President, marking the beginning of the interim period during which the South would administer itself and prepare for the independence referendum. GoSS faced enormous capacity challenges — managing one of the world's least-developed territories with an oil-revenue-dependent budget and minimal state infrastructure.

title: SPLM Suspends Participation in National Unity Government
description: The SPLM temporarily suspended its participation in the Government of National Unity in Khartoum in October 2007, accusing the National Congress Party of failing to implement key CPA provisions — including Abyei boundary demarcation, troop redeployment, and the national wealth-sharing formula. The suspension highlighted the fragility of CPA implementation and previewed the near-collapse of the process.

title: Abyei Crisis — SAF and SPLA Clash at Oil-Rich Border Town
description: Sudanese Armed Forces and SPLA clashed in May 2008 in the disputed oil-rich Abyei region, with Khartoum's forces seizing and burning much of Abyei town and displacing 60,000 civilians. The Abyei crisis nearly derailed the entire CPA process and required intensive international mediation, resulting in the Abyei Roadmap Agreement and the eventual deployment of UNISFA peacekeepers.

title: ICC Issues Arrest Warrant for Al-Bashir for Darfur Atrocities
description: The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir in March 2009 for war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Darfur — the first sitting head of state indicted by the ICC. The warrant increased Khartoum's isolation and complicated CPA implementation by hardening al-Bashir's refusal to comply with international demands.

title: Sudan Presidential and Parliamentary Elections
description: Sudan held its first multi-party elections since 1986 in April 2010 under CPA provisions, with al-Bashir winning the presidential race and Salva Kiir winning the southern Sudan presidency with over 92% of the vote amid widespread reports of fraud and SPLM dominance. The elections locked in both leaders ahead of the independence referendum and established SPLM's monopoly on southern political power.

title: Independence Referendum — 98.83% Vote for Secession
description: South Sudan held its independence referendum from January 9–15, 2011, with 98.83% of voters choosing independence from Sudan in a result internationally recognized as credible despite logistical difficulties. Turnout exceeded 97% among registered voters, reflecting near-universal popular support for secession, and the result was accepted by President al-Bashir in a statement in Khartoum.

title: South Sudan Independence Declared — World's Newest Nation
description: South Sudan declared independence on July 9, 2011, becoming the world's newest internationally recognized state and the 54th member of the African Union, with Salva Kiir as President and Riek Machar as Vice President. The celebration in Juba was attended by dozens of world leaders, and the United States and UN immediately recognized the new state, though the country inherited massive underdevelopment, landlocked geography, oil dependency, and unresolved border disputes.

title: South Sudan Joins United Nations
description: South Sudan was admitted as the 193rd member of the United Nations on July 14, 2011, just five days after independence, in an unprecedented rapid admission reflecting near-universal international support for the new state. UNMISS (UN Mission in South Sudan) was simultaneously established to support peace consolidation, replacing the previous UNMIS mandate.

title: Oil Shutdown — South Sudan Halts Production in Revenue Dispute
description: South Sudan shut down its entire oil production in January 2012 after failing to reach agreement with Sudan over transit fees for using the pipeline and infrastructure to Port Sudan, costing both countries hundreds of millions of dollars monthly in lost revenue. The shutdown lasted over a year and triggered a severe economic crisis, with South Sudan's budget — 98% oil-dependent — collapsing and hyperinflation beginning.

title: Heglig Border Crisis — South Sudan Seizes Sudanese Oil Town
description: South Sudan's SPLA briefly seized Heglig (Panthou), an oil-producing town inside Sudan's internationally recognized territory, in April 2012, triggering airstrikes by Sudan's air force and international condemnation including from the UN Security Council. South Sudan withdrew under pressure after 10 days, but the incident brought the two countries to the brink of full-scale war and further poisoned post-independence relations.

title: Addis Ababa Economic Cooperation Agreements Signed
description: Under intense African Union mediation, Sudan and South Sudan signed a package of nine cooperation agreements in Addis Ababa in September 2012, covering oil transit fees, border trade, currency, banking, and security, partially resolving the disputes that had caused the oil shutdown. Oil production gradually resumed, but implementation of the agreements remained incomplete.

title: Kiir Dismisses Machar and Cabinet — Political Crisis Deepens
description: President Salva Kiir dismissed Vice President Riek Machar and the entire cabinet in July 2013, accusing Machar of plotting a coup and effectively ending the SPLM's post-independence power-sharing arrangement. The dismissal shattered the fragile political equilibrium between Dinka and Nuer factions within the SPLM and set the stage for armed conflict.

title: Civil War Erupts — Juba Massacres Mark Dinka-Nuer Conflict
description: South Sudan's devastating civil war began on December 15–16, 2013, when fighting broke out in Juba between Presidential Guard (Dinka) units and soldiers loyal to Machar (Nuer), triggering ethnically targeted killings of Nuer civilians in Juba and spreading rapidly to Upper Nile, Unity, and Jonglei states. The conflict — framed by Kiir as a coup attempt and by Machar as an ethnic purge — killed tens of thousands in its first weeks and displaced over a million people within months.

title: Bentiu Massacre — Ethnic Killings at UN Compound Vicinity
description: Forces loyal to Riek Machar killed hundreds of civilians — predominantly ethnic Dinka, Darfuri, and others — at Bentiu in Unity State in April 2014, with radio broadcasts used to incite ethnic violence in one of the worst single atrocities of the civil war. The UN Human Rights Commission documented the killings as potential crimes against humanity, and the incident drew international calls for accountability.

title: IGAD Ceasefire Agreements Repeatedly Violated
description: IGAD brokered multiple ceasefire agreements between the Kiir government and Machar's SPLM-IO in 2014, all of which collapsed within days as both sides accused each other of violations. The failed ceasefires exposed the limits of regional mediation without enforcement mechanisms and allowed the conflict to metastasize from a political crisis into an entrenched ethnic war.

title: Famine Warning — UN Declares Humanitarian Emergency
description: The UN declared a humanitarian emergency in South Sudan in early 2014, warning of impending famine conditions as the civil war disrupted agriculture, displaced over 1.5 million people, and blocked aid access across conflict zones. The crisis marked the beginning of a sustained humanitarian catastrophe that would intermittently reach formal famine classification in subsequent years.

title: ARCSS Peace Agreement Signed Under Pressure
description: The Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in South Sudan (ARCSS) was signed in Addis Ababa on August 17, 2015, after IGAD threatened sanctions and the US imposed targeted sanctions on senior officials from both sides. The agreement reinstated Machar as First Vice President and established a Transitional Government of National Unity (TGoNU), but was signed under duress by Kiir who immediately appended 16 reservations.

title: Machar Returns to Juba — TGoNU Formed
description: Riek Machar returned to Juba in April 2016 and was sworn in as First Vice President, inaugurating the Transitional Government of National Unity envisioned by the ARCSS. The political settlement appeared fragile from the outset as armed forces of both factions remained in Juba and mutual distrust ran deep.

title: July 2016 Juba Fighting — ARCSS Collapses, Machar Flees
description: Heavy fighting erupted in Juba's presidential compound and across the city on July 7–11, 2016, killing hundreds including UN peacekeepers and aid workers, in a direct confrontation between Kiir's and Machar's forces that effectively ended the ARCSS. Machar fled first to DRC and then through CAR and Sudan into exile, and Kiir replaced him with Taban Deng Gai, collapsing the peace agreement within weeks of its implementation.

title: Malakal Protection of Civilians Site Attacks
description: Government-allied forces attacked the UN Protection of Civilians (PoC) site at Malakal in February 2016, killing at least 18 internally displaced persons and wounding dozens in a direct assault on a protected humanitarian space. The attack highlighted the failure of the Juba peace process and the vulnerability of civilians sheltering under UN protection.

title: UN Declares Famine in Unity State
description: The UN formally declared famine in parts of Unity State in February 2017 — the first formal famine declaration anywhere in the world since 2011 — with 100,000 people facing starvation and 1 million on the brink. The famine was primarily driven by the civil war's disruption of agriculture and deliberate obstruction of humanitarian access rather than drought alone.

title: Arms Embargo Debates at UN Security Council
description: The UN Security Council debated a comprehensive arms embargo on South Sudan throughout 2017, with the US and European states pushing for restrictions while Russia and China blocked a binding resolution. A watered-down compromise maintained monitoring mechanisms but failed to cut off weapons flows to both government and opposition forces.

title: Revitalized ARCSS (R-ARCSS) Signed in Addis Ababa
description: A revitalized peace agreement (R-ARCSS) was signed in Addis Ababa on September 12, 2018, between Kiir's government, Machar's SPLM-IO, and other armed groups, establishing a new Transitional Government of National Unity and a 35-month transition period ahead of elections. The R-ARCSS was brokered by the IGAD High Level Revitalization Forum and backed by the AU and UN, though critics noted that it replicated many ARCSS provisions that had already failed.

title: Khartoum Declaration Between Kiir and Machar
description: South Sudan's President Kiir and opposition leader Machar signed the Khartoum Declaration in Sudan in July 2018 (with implementation continuing through 2019), agreeing to a permanent ceasefire and unification of forces as prerequisites for forming the revitalized transitional government. The declaration reduced fighting significantly in most regions but left security arrangements contentious.

title: Transitional Government of National Unity Inaugurated
description: The Revitalized Transitional Government of National Unity (RTGoNU) was inaugurated on February 22, 2020, with Machar returning to Juba and being sworn in as First Vice President for the third time — completing the political settlement envisioned by the R-ARCSS after repeated deadline extensions. The government faced immediate implementation challenges including incomplete cantonment of forces, lack of state-level appointments, and a severe budget crisis worsened by low oil prices.

title: COVID-19 and Economic Collapse Worsen Humanitarian Crisis
description: The COVID-19 pandemic reached South Sudan in April 2020 amid an already catastrophic humanitarian situation — 7.5 million people food insecure, the pound at historic lows, and oil revenues collapsing due to the global price crash. The government declared a state of emergency, imposed curfews, and international aid deliveries were severely disrupted, compounding the crisis for one of the world's most aid-dependent populations.

title: Catastrophic Flooding Displaces Hundreds of Thousands
description: South Sudan experienced its worst flooding in decades in 2020, with the Nile and its tributaries inundating large parts of Jonglei, Unity, Upper Nile, and Lakes states, displacing over 800,000 people and destroying crops across the country's most productive agricultural zones. The floods were driven by above-average Indian Ocean rainfall linked to climate variability and compounded by the country's lack of drainage infrastructure.

title: Ongoing Intercommunal Violence in Jonglei and Greater Pibor
description: Intercommunal violence between Murle, Lou Nuer, and Dinka cattle-herding communities in Jonglei and the Greater Pibor Administrative Area killed thousands in 2021, with raids targeting civilians, abducting children, and destroying villages in cycles of revenge that state security forces were unable or unwilling to halt. The violence underscored the RTGoNU's limited territorial authority and the fragility of the 2020 peace settlement outside Juba.

title: Elections Postponed — Transition Period Extended
description: South Sudan's 2022 elections — promised under the R-ARCSS — were postponed in 2021 as the RTGoNU cited unfulfilled security, constitutional, and census prerequisites, extending the transition period by two additional years to 2024. The postponement, agreed between Kiir and Machar, was criticized by civil society and donors as a mechanism to entrench incumbency.

title: Renewed Flooding — Third Consecutive Year of Catastrophic Inundation
description: For the third consecutive year, South Sudan experienced extreme flooding in 2022, affecting over 900,000 people and submerging large portions of Jonglei, Unity, and Upper Nile — exceeding the previous year's disaster in scale. The multi-year flooding pattern was attributed to La Niña and the ongoing degradation of the Sudd wetland buffer, raising questions about long-term habitability in affected regions.

title: Famine Conditions Return — 8.3 Million Food Insecure
description: The UN's Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) reported in 2022 that 8.3 million South Sudanese — two-thirds of the population — faced acute food insecurity at crisis level or worse, with catastrophic conditions (IPC Phase 5) in parts of Jonglei. The combination of conflict, flooding, economic collapse, and COVID-related supply disruptions produced a food crisis of unprecedented breadth.

title: Sudan War Erupts — Refugee Influx and Pipeline Disruption
description: The outbreak of war between Sudan's SAF and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in April 2023 sent hundreds of thousands of refugees fleeing into South Sudan — reversing decades of refugee flow — and threatened the Greater Nile Oil Pipeline running through Sudan that carries South Sudan's entire oil export revenue. South Sudan, already fiscally fragile, faced simultaneous refugee pressure and the risk of losing its primary source of income if pipeline infrastructure was damaged.

title: South Sudan Oil Revenue Crisis Deepens Amid Sudan Conflict
description: The Sudan war directly disrupted South Sudan's oil export revenues as fighting damaged pipeline infrastructure and halted operations at Port Sudan, reducing oil export income at a time when South Sudan's currency had already lost over 90% of its value since 2015. The government cut public sector salaries to near zero in real terms, and the humanitarian funding gap widened as donor fatigue increased.

title: UNMISS Mandate Extended — Security Sector Reform Stalled
description: The UN Security Council extended the UNMISS mandate in 2023 with 17,000 authorized personnel, as South Sudan's Necessary Unified Forces (NUF) — the force meant to replace factional armies under the R-ARCSS — remained far below graduation targets due to funding shortfalls and political obstruction. The security sector reform failure was identified by UN monitors as the principal structural risk to the peace process.

title: Elections Postponed Again to December 2026
description: South Sudan's political parties agreed in 2024 to postpone national elections again — originally due in 2023 then 2024 — to December 2026, citing the absence of a permanent constitution, a completed national census, voter registration, and unified security forces. International observers warned that repeated postponements risked permanently entrenching the transitional government without democratic accountability.

title: Sustained Refugee Crisis from Sudan Overwhelms Border Communities
description: By mid-2024, over 700,000 people — mostly South Sudanese returnees and Sudanese refugees — had crossed into South Sudan fleeing the Sudan war, constituting one of the fastest-growing displacement crises globally and placing enormous strain on Renk and Maban counties in Upper Nile State. The UNHCR warned that host community resources were exhausted and called for $1.7 billion in emergency funding.

title: Violence in Upper Nile and Warrap — Peace Fragility Exposed
description: Renewed intercommunal and politically motivated violence erupted in Upper Nile and Warrap states in 2024, with clashes between armed youth groups and government forces killing hundreds and displacing tens of thousands, undermining the 2020 peace settlement's credibility ahead of the already-delayed elections. Human rights monitors documented extrajudicial killings by security forces responding to the unrest.

title: South Sudan Ranked Among World's Most Fragile States
description: South Sudan ranked first or second globally on multiple fragility and humanitarian risk indices in 2024, including the Fragile States Index and the INFORM Risk Index, reflecting a sustained combination of conflict, governance failure, economic collapse, climate vulnerability, and humanitarian catastrophe. With over 9 million people facing acute food insecurity and a constitutional vacuum, analysts assessed the country as facing simultaneous compounding crises with no near-term resolution.
